title: Reversible rules are rare among cellular automata

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Reversible rules are rare among cellular automata

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Reversibility is rare among simple cellular automaton rules: only 6 of the 256 elementary two-color nearest-neighbor rules are reversible, and only 1800 of the 7,625,597,484,987 three-color nearest-neighbor rules are.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: There are a total of 7,625,597,484,987 cellular automata with three colors and nearest-neighbor rules, and searching through these one finds just 1800 that are reversible.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 9, “Fundamental Physics”; section “The Notion of Reversibility” (from p. 435), p. 436. Scope: one-dimensional cellular automata with two and three colors and nearest-neighbor rules

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch09-02: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.95

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim gives exact finite rule classes and exact counts, making it completely operational. Rule definitions are public and reversibility has mathematical decision procedures and structural classifications. A checkable proof or optimized enumeration can settle the statement without new empirical data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Formally define reversibility on the intended lattice or finite periodic configurations, classify all binary elementary rules analytically, and verify the three-color count with a checkable enumeration or theorem. Counts other than 6 and 1800 under the stated convention refute the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Naive enumeration of trillions of rules is infeasible without structural reductions.

Reversibility conventions for infinite versus finite periodic configurations must match the stated counts.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

data adequacy: 0.98
data existence: 1.0
operationalizability: 0.98
discriminating power: 1.0

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Both numbers are exact claims about finite, fully specified rule spaces. The two-color count is a few seconds of computation, and the three-color count is a known decision procedure applied to a large but finite set, feasible for a small team with a cluster in weeks rather than a missing dataset. A discrepancy in either count would refute the claim.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Decide reversibility for each of the 256 two-color nearest-neighbor rules and for each of the 7,625,597,484,987 three-color nearest-neighbor rules, using a fixed injectivity test, and count the reversible cases. Exactly six and exactly 1800 would confirm the claim; any other counts would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Reversibility on the infinite line, on periodic lattices, and on finite strings need not coincide, so the predicate must match the one used for the count of 1800.

The three-color space is trillions of rules; the test is finite but large.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Among one-dimensional nearest-neighbour cellular automata, exactly 6 of the 256 two-colour rules and exactly 1800 of the 3^27 = 7,625,597,484,987 three-colour rules are reversible, where reversible means the global map on bi-infinite configurations is injective (equivalently bijective; equivalently, by Wolfram's note, all periodic configurations have distinct successors).

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py compiles revca.c and runs the exhaustive depth-first enumeration of rule tables for (k,r) = (2,1), (2,2) and (3,1). Table entries are assigned in order of the period of their neighbourhood word; after each assignment the pair graph of the de Bruijn graph is built from definite edges (both labels assigned and equal) and the branch is cut if an off-diagonal cycle or a diagonal-to-diagonal path through off-diagonal nodes exists (both are sound: they witness two distinct configurations with the same image); the balance condition (each colour exactly k^(2r) times) also prunes. At a leaf the same test is exact. The 1800 rules found for k = 3 are then checked in Python with Wolfram's ReversibleQ (distinct successors of all cyclic configurations of length <= 9), 10000 random balanced k = 3 tables not in the list are checked to fail it, all 256 elementary rules are classified by both methods, and the k = 3 rules are grouped into symmetry families under colour permutations and reflection.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. An exhaustive enumeration with an exact injectivity test (pair graph of the de Bruijn graph: a rule is injective iff the pair graph has no cycle through an off-diagonal node and no diagonal-to-diagonal path through off-diagonal nodes; used both as a sound pruning condition during depth-first assignment of the rule table and as the exact test at the leaves) yields exactly 6 reversible rules for k = 2, r = 1 and exactly 1800 for k = 3, r = 1. As a check of the method, the same program must give 62 for k = 2, r = 2 (NKS note 'Numbers of reversible rules'), and the 6 elementary rules must be {15, 51, 85, 170, 204, 240}. Also, every rule found must pass Wolfram's finite test (distinct successors for all periodic configurations of period <= 9, as his note says suffices for k = 3) and every rule not found that is sampled (10000 random balanced k = 3 rules) must fail it. 'Supports' requires the counts 6 and 1800 and the consistency checks.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if the exhaustive enumeration completes and gives a count other than 6 for k = 2, r = 1 or other than 1800 for k = 3, r = 1 (with the k = 2, r = 2 check giving 62, so the method is validated). If the k = 3 enumeration cannot be completed within the compute budget (about 1 hour), the verdict is 'mixed' or 'inconclusive' (reason: other) with the k = 2 result and a lower bound on the k = 3 count reported.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: reversible rules among the 3^27 three-colour nearest-neighbour cellular automata (claimed 1800)

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: 'Reversible' is taken as injectivity of the global map on the full shift (bi-infinite configurations), the standard notion and the one Wolfram's note tests through periodic configurations. Rule numbering is Wolfram's (table entry for neighbourhood (l,c,r) at digit position l*k^2 + c*k + r of the base-k rule number). The count is of raw rule tables, not of symmetry classes (the note gives 172 families for k = 3). The enumeration is exact, so there is no sampling uncertainty; the only risks are implementation errors, which the k = 2 (r = 1 and r = 2) checks and the independent periodic-configuration test guard against. Note: the pruning search is written in C (compiled with gcc from analysis.py) because a Python search over the pruned tree would be too slow; this is a deviation from 'python3 only' tooling and is recorded.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
Exhaustive enumeration of nearest-neighbour cellular automaton rules (generated by analysis.py + revca.c)

NKS notes 'Numbers of reversible rules' and 'Testing for reversibility' (p. 1017)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The search is written in C (revca.c) and analysis.py compiles it with gcc; this is a tooling deviation from the python-only guideline, recorded in the pre-registration. The search visits 25.7 million nodes for k = 3 (about 2 minutes).

Correctness of the pair-graph criterion is checked three ways: it reproduces the known 6 elementary rules and Wolfram's 62 for k = 2, r = 2; all 256 elementary rules are classified identically by the independent periodic-configuration test; and all 1800 three-colour rules found pass that test while 10000 random balanced tables outside the list fail it. The count of 172 symmetry families also matches Wolfram's note.

Reversibility is tested on bi-infinite configurations (the full shift). On finite cyclic lattices of a fixed size a rule can be a bijection without being reversible in this sense; the claim and Wolfram's own test use the infinite-line notion.

The total 7,625,597,484,987 = 3^27 is a count of rule tables, confirmed arithmetically; the enumeration does not visit them individually but prunes soundly, so the count 1800 is exact.
